subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: Periodicity & Energetics — Nov–Dec window review (Structure 3.1 + Reactivity 1)

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the arrangement of the periodic table?
choices: Periods are the vertical columns of elements with similar chemical properties.
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.
The f-block elements occur only in periods 6 and 7.
Metalloids are found exclusively in period 3.
items.note: Groups are vertical columns; elements in the same group share the same number of valence electrons and similar properties. Periods are horizontal rows. The f-block is the lanthanides and actinides. Metalloids lie along the diagonal staircase, not only in one period. Trap: confusing the orientation of periods and groups.

items.stem: What is the condensed electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16)?
items.note: Sulfur is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴. Argon is the noble-gas core for elements after Z = 18. Trap: incorrect p-electron count or wrong noble-gas core.

items.stem: Which element has the anomalous electron configuration [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵?
items.note: Chromium adopts [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ (half-filled 3d subshell) rather than the expected [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴. Vanadium is 4s² 3d³, manganese is 4s² 3d⁵. Trap: applying the simple Aufbau order without the known exception.

items.stem: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period because
choices: the number of electron shells increases
nuclear charge increases while shielding remains approximately constant
electrons are added to a new principal shell
items.note: Across a period protons are added to the same shell; the increased nuclear attraction outweighs the roughly constant shielding, pulling the electron cloud closer. Trap: confusing the across-period trend with the down-group trend in which new shells are added.

items.stem: The first three successive ionization energies of an element are 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ mol⁻¹. The element is most likely
items.note: A large jump after the second ionization energy shows that the third electron is removed from a new, inner shell, consistent with two valence electrons (Mg). Sodium shows the jump after the first IE; aluminium after the third. Trap: miscounting which ionization produces the jump.

items.stem: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group principally because
choices: atomic radius decreases and effective nuclear charge increases across a period
the total number of electrons increases
items.note: Smaller atomic radius and higher effective nuclear charge allow the nucleus to attract a bonding pair of electrons more strongly. Trap: attributing the trend simply to ‘more electrons’ without considering size and Z_eff.

items.stem: Metallic character increases down a group because
choices: atoms become larger and the outer electrons are more easily lost
nuclear charge increases without any change in size
shielding decreases while the number of shells increases
items.note: Larger atoms have outer electrons farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more readily, increasing metallic character. Trap: focusing only on increasing nuclear charge while ignoring the dominant size effect.

items.stem: In an exothermic reaction
choices: ΔH is positive and the products have higher enthalpy than the reactants
ΔH is negative and heat is released to the surroundings
items.note: Exothermic processes release heat; the system loses enthalpy so ΔH < 0. Trap: reversing the sign convention for ΔH.

items.stem: On an energy-profile diagram the activation energy is
choices: the difference in enthalpy between reactants and products
the energy difference between the reactants and the transition state
always equal in magnitude to ΔH
items.note: Activation energy is the barrier from reactants to the transition state (activated complex). ΔH is the net enthalpy change from reactants to products. Trap: equating Ea with ΔH.

items.stem: When 0.50 g of a compound (M = 50 g mol⁻¹) is completely burned, the heat released raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 15 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹). The enthalpy of combustion is closest to
items.note: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 15 = 6270 J = 6.27 kJ for 0.01 mol, giving ΔHc ≈ −627 kJ mol⁻¹. Trap: omitting the conversion to moles or the negative sign required for combustion.

items.stem: Using the average bond enthalpies C–H 412, C=O 743, O–H 463 and O=O 496 kJ mol⁻¹, the enthalpy change for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O is approximately
items.note: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = (4 × 412 + 2 × 496) − (2 × 743 + 4 × 463) ≈ −700 kJ mol⁻¹. Trap: reversing the sign or miscounting the O–H bonds formed.

items.stem: Given ΔHf°(CO₂) = −394, ΔHf°(H₂O) = −286 and ΔHf°(CH₄) = −75 kJ mol⁻¹, the standard enthalpy of combustion of methane is
items.note: ΔHc = [ΔHf(CO₂) + 2ΔHf(H₂O)] − ΔHf(CH₄) = (−394 − 572) − (−75) = −891 kJ mol⁻¹. Trap: adding the enthalpies of formation instead of subtracting reactants, or forgetting the stoichiometric coefficient for water.

items.stem: The electron configuration of Fe²⁺ (Z = 26) is
items.note: Neutral Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; the 4s electrons are lost first to form Fe²⁺, leaving [Ar] 3d⁶. Trap: removing electrons from the 3d subshell or retaining the 4s electrons.

items.stem: In the orbital box diagram for the 2p sublevel of a nitrogen atom the electrons are arranged as
choices: all three electrons paired in a single orbital
three unpaired electrons in three separate orbitals
two paired electrons and one unpaired electron
all electrons placed in the 2s orbital
items.note: Hund’s rule requires that electrons occupy separate orbitals of the same energy with parallel spins before pairing; nitrogen’s 2p³ configuration therefore has three unpaired electrons. Trap: pairing electrons prematurely against Hund’s rule.

items.stem: First ionization energy generally increases across a period because
choices: effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases
a new electron shell is added
items.note: Higher effective nuclear charge and smaller atomic radius make the outer electron harder to remove. Trap: confusing the across-period increase with the decrease that occurs down a group.

items.stem: Which ion has the largest ionic radius?
items.note: O²⁻ is an anion with a larger electron cloud; the cations Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ are isoelectronic but successive increases in nuclear charge pull the remaining electrons closer. Trap: assuming higher nuclear charge always produces the smallest ion without considering the difference between anions and cations.

items.stem: An endothermic reaction has
choices: ΔH negative and heat absorbed from the surroundings
ΔH positive and heat absorbed from the surroundings
products lower in enthalpy than the reactants
items.note: Endothermic processes absorb heat; the system gains enthalpy so ΔH > 0. Trap: reversing the sign convention for ΔH.

items.stem: Average bond enthalpy is defined as
choices: the energy required to break one mole of a specific bond in one particular gaseous molecule
the mean energy required to break one mole of a given bond type averaged over a range of gaseous molecules
identical to the standard enthalpy of formation
items.note: Average bond enthalpies are mean values obtained from many different compounds containing that bond in the gaseous state. Trap: treating the average value as the exact bond-dissociation energy of a single molecule.

items.stem: For the reaction 2C + O₂ → 2CO, using ΔHc(C) = −394 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔHc(CO) = −283 kJ mol⁻¹, the enthalpy change is
items.note: ΔH = 2 × ΔHc(C) − 2 × ΔHc(CO) = 2(−394) − 2(−283) = −222 kJ. Trap: omitting the stoichiometric coefficients or reversing the sign when applying Hess’s law to combustion data.

items.stem: According to the Aufbau principle electrons occupy
items.note: The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy. Trap: reversing the energy order.

items.stem: Explain why the first ionization energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen, contrary to the general increase across a period. Refer to electron configurations.
markscheme: In oxygen one 2p orbital contains a pair of electrons (1)
Electron–electron repulsion in that paired orbital makes removal of an electron easier (1)
Nitrogen’s half-filled 2p³ subshell is especially stable, so its IE is higher (1)
items.tactic: Write both electron configurations, identify the paired electrons in oxygen’s 2p subshell, and link the repulsion (and the stability of nitrogen’s half-filled subshell) directly to the lower ionization energy.

items.stem: Calculate the enthalpy change for C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ using the average bond enthalpies C=C 614, C–C 346, C–H 412 and H–H 436 kJ mol⁻¹. Show your working.
markscheme: Negative sign and correct units stated (1)
items.tactic: Identify precisely which bonds break (the C=C double bond and the H–H bond) and which form (the new C–C single bond and two additional C–H bonds). Apply ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) and include the sign and units.
